newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM calls for end to race criticism. [CORRECTED 01:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Australian PM calls for end to race criticism. [CORRECTED 01:15 GMT]

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard, persistently under fire over race issues in recent months, has called for an end to "unreasonable criticism" of the country's racism record.

"I think it is time we called an end to the self-flagellation, the introspection, the defensiveness and the willingness to accept unfounded criticism, unjustified criticism of the performance of the Australian nation," Howard told a Liberal Party dinner on Tuesday night.

"We can look any people in the eye and say we have done right by our citizens by any measure of international behaviour and I, as prime minister of Australia, am no longer prepared to accept unreasonable, ill-founded and uninformed criticism of the tolerance credentials of the Australian community."
His call came as violent protests greeted the launch of the Canberra branch of race row politician Pauline Hanson's One Nation party on Tuesday night.

Hanson, a Queenland independent who has attracted a nation-wide following on an anti-immigration platform, has vowed to continue rallying party support despite the increasingly violent protests against her party's launches.

Two protesters were arrested at a rowdy anti-Hanson demonstration in the Australian capital of Canberra on Tuesday night, a day after another launch meeting for the party descended into violence in a country town near Melbourne.

In recent days two former prime ministers, one from Howard's Liberal party, have criticised Howard for not showing sufficient leadership in the race debate and for not making a national apology to tens of thousands of Aborigines stolen from their parents under a past policy of forced assimilation.

Former Labor prime minister Gough Whitlam (corrects from Liberal prime minister Malcolm Fraser) said on Monday that Howard's failure to repudiate Hanson was another example of "the folly of ignoring or postponing a problem in the hope that it would disappear or diminish".
In a television interview on Tuesday, Hanson herself said the violence at her party meetings only made her more determined to carry on.
Hanson did not attend either rally this week but is to visit a party meeting in another country town, Geelong, next week. Opinion polls put support for Hanson at between six and 10 percent.
